doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Count Basie band and Thad Jones
title: Joining Basie as lead trumpet after Basie's death
summary: He went from Woody Herman's band straight into the lead chair just after Basie died, when Eric Dixon ran the band and prices dropped until Thad Jones was hired.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Did you step into the lead chair?
Um hum. Right to a lead chair. I had come right from Woody Herman’s band.
And Thad Jones was conducting at that time?

Yeah actually I got there at a pivotal period. I got there right when Basie had died. And then Eric Dixon was the conductor. I don’t know if you know Eric but he was a great tenor player in the band. He was Straw Boss during the later years. And it’s a great sort of lesson about, I don’t know if it’s too trivial to tell on the tape, but a lesson about sort of business. It’s always nice to observe stuff. Basie died and the guys said we want to keep the band going, let’s try to keep it going. Eric Dixon is Straw Boss okay, I’ll count off the tunes and I’ll announce them, but we’ll sort of not have a leader, I’ll just count off tunes and announce. It won’t be a big deal. Basie was never really an out-front man, he just played and he said a couple of things. We’ll run it like that. Well the nostalgia of it kept for about six months and they could keep the gigs and maybe they’d cut off a little bit of the money from the price that they were getting, because Basie was booked for probably a year into his death. So they kept the same gigs. But then after six months the prices started going down, because the nostalgia, okay, he’s passed on. The band’s probably not any good. So the prices get lower, and there’s no out front person, no person to say — because it’s funny, I realized I don’t mean to keep talking about business things — you know I even realized that like I was in the Basie band on and off for almost four years. And it’s one humbling thing as a musician to go somewhere and I’d been playing with them for four years, I went to New York and I’d visit New York and people would say, “What you doing?” I’d say, “I’m playing with the Basie band, you don’t know that?” And they’re like, “No, are they still going?” And you’re like wait a minute, I just got a standing ovation in Iowa last night. So you have to have really a lot of strength as an artist. Look I played at Hamilton College last night, and hopefully people enjoyed it, but nobody else knows about that then these people at Hamilton. So you have to have a lot of strength, because you think your name is getting out there in the people. It’s a long process. That’s what was happening to the Basie band. They needed some national press, and they didn’t have one person to center in on, a star person. So they found out they had to get somebody, so they hired Thad Jones.
